# Introduction

DDSA splits the log-likelihood into three parts: the infection-time Multinomial term $\ell_I$, the recovery-interval phase-type term $\ell_R$, and the Binomial final-size constraint $\ell_\text{constr}$. Each piece contributes different information about transmission. In practice, line lists are often incomplete: contact-tracing programmes may capture infection onset times without follow-up on recovery, or hospital records may provide recovery durations without precise transmission dates. This notebook measures what each likelihood component contributes by fitting DDSA under three data-availability scenarios on one synthetic line list ($N=99$, $\rho=0.01$, $\Delta t=1$\,d, $T=40$\,d). In every scenario, we compare three infectious-period models: GLCT, Boxcar, and Geometric.

| Scenario | Observed data | Likelihood | Parameters identified |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| A — Full | Infection times, recovery intervals, final size | $\ell_I + \ell_R + \ell_\text{constr}$ | $\beta$, $\rho$, $r$, $p$; mean IP $= r/p$ |
| B — Infection only | Infection times and final size | $\ell_I + \ell_\text{constr}$ | $R_0$, $\rho$, mean IP (weakly); $r$ poorly identified |
| C — Recovery only | Recovery intervals | $\ell_R$ | $r$, $p$; $\beta$ and $\rho$ not identifiable |

The simulator uses a continuous Erlang infectious period with mean $\mu=4$\,d, then embeds it in discrete time at $\Delta t=1$\,d using per-step transition probabilities from constant hazards (i.e. $p = 1-e^{-r\Delta t}$). This discretisation increases the mean relative to the continuous target: in the discrete model, the expected infectious duration is $E[W]\approx 6.33$\,d (for $\mu=4$\,d at $\Delta t=1$\,d). We therefore use $E[W]$, not $\mu$, as the reference for posterior comparisons. We calibrate transmission as $\beta_\text{rate}=R_0^\text{cal}/\mu=0.5$\,d$^{-1}$ (with $R_0^\text{cal}=2$), which implies a discrete-time reproduction number $R_0^\text{imp}=\beta_\text{true}\times E[W]=3.164$. That value is the target when comparing posterior $R_0=\beta\cdot r/p$. Inference uses a flexible NegBin-DPH parameterisation $(r,p)$ with mean IP $=r/p$, and does not force $r$ to match the simulator’s Erlang stage count $k=4$.

In Scenario B, the NegBin shape $r$ is not identifiable from incidence alone: many $(r, p, R_0)$ combinations generate almost the same epidemic trajectory. We therefore sum the likelihood over $r \in \{1, \ldots, 10\}$, as in Scenarios A and C, and report its posterior rather than choosing a single value. Because the meaning of $p$ changes with $r$ (mean IP $= r/p$), Scenario B samples $R_0$ and the mean infectious period $\mu$ directly and sets $p = r/\mu$ and $\beta = R_0/\mu$, so the real-valued parameters keep the same meaning for every $r$. The Geometric sub-scenario ($r\equiv1$) has no $r$ to sum over.

## Libraries

The analysis uses Turing.jl for Bayesian inference and the shared `PhaseTypeDistributions.jl` module (repository root) for discrete phase-type distributions. The integer phase count $r$ is summed out of the likelihood with the shared `IntegerParameters.jl` helpers, so no Gibbs or Metropolis–Hastings steps are needed.

```{julia}

#| output: false
```

## Parameters

Here we define simulation settings and build the discrete DPH used to generate the synthetic data (daily line list, $Δt=1$\,d, horizon $T=40$\,d). The printed output reports the effective discrete mean ($E[W]$), the infectious-period coefficient of variation ($CV$), and the implied reproduction number ($R_0^\text{imp}=\beta_\text{true}\times E[W]$), which is the reference target used in the results.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

R0_cal = 2.0       # continuous calibration target; β_rate = R0_cal/μ_ip
ρ_true = 0.01
μ_ip   = 4.0       # continuous Erlang mean (not the discrete E[W])
k      = 4         # Erlang stages in simulator
Δt_nom = 1.0       # one MCMC/map step = one day; per-stage g = 1 - exp(-(k/μ_ip)*Δt_nom)
tspan  = (0.0, 40.0)
nsteps = Int(round(tspan[2] / Δt_nom))

β_rate = R0_cal / μ_ip             # day^-1; before dwell discretisation
β_true = β_rate * Δt_nom           # per-step coefficient in simulate_discrete_glct
β_prior_hi = 2.5                   # upper bound for β ~ Uniform(1e-4, β_prior_hi) 


dph_nom = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_erlang_from_mean(k, μ_ip, Δt_nom)
nb_r    = k                        # shape of the continuous simulator Erlang k 
nb_mean = PhaseTypeDistributions.mean(dph_nom)   # discrete E[W]
nb_cv   = sqrt(PhaseTypeDistributions.var(dph_nom)) / nb_mean  # coefficient of variation
nb_p    = k / μ_ip                 # continuous Erlang rate (as reference)
R0_imp = β_true * nb_mean          # Implied R₀: R₀_imp = β × E[W] (discrete)

K_age   = findfirst(kk -> PhaseTypeDistributions.cdf(dph_nom, kk) >= 0.999, 1:500)

```

```{julia}
        "CV = $(round(nb_cv, digits=3)), β_true = $(β_true)/step")
println("  R₀_cal = $R0_cal uses μ_ip only for β_rate = R₀_cal/μ_ip (does not equal β_true×E[W]).")
```

## Utility functions

In this we section define the helper functions used across all scenarios: safe normalisation of incidence probability vectors, conversion of rates to per-step proportions, discrete hazard computation from phase-type and standard distributions.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""Safely normalise a non-negative vector to sum to 1."""
function safe_normalise(f::AbstractVector{T}, n::Int) where T
    f_pos = ifelse.(isnan.(f) .| .!isfinite.(f), zero(T), max.(f, zero(T)))
    sF = sum(f_pos)
    (sF > T(1e-15) && isfinite(sF)) ? f_pos ./ sF : fill(one(T)/n, n)
end

"""Shared x-axis limits for mean infectious period (r/p) KDE plots: zoom to pooled quantiles."""
function mean_ip_density_xlims(vectors...; qlo=0.03, qhi=0.97, pad_frac=0.06)
    parts = [vec(v) for v in vectors if length(v) > 0]
    isempty(parts) && return (0.0, 15.0)
    v = reduce(vcat, parts)
    lo, hi = quantile(v, qlo), quantile(v, qhi)
    pad = max(pad_frac * (hi - lo), 0.5)
    return (max(0.0, lo - pad), hi + pad)
end

"""Convert a rate to a proportion over a unit time interval."""
@inline function rate_to_proportion(r, t=1.0)
    if r < 0 || isnan(r)
        return 0.0
    elseif isinf(r)
        return 1.0
    else
        result = 1 - exp(-r * t)
        return isnan(result) ? 0.0 : max(min(result, 1.0), 0.0)
    end
end

"""Discrete hazard h[k] = P(W=k)/P(W≥k) for NegBin(r,p) parameters; AD-compatible.

Computed on the log scale, h[k] = exp(log P(W=k) − log P(W≥k)). In the far tail both
probabilities underflow, and the ratio pmf/sf then has a 0/0 derivative (NaN gradients
under ForwardDiff) even though its value is harmless."""
function hazard_vector_negbin(nb_r::Integer, nb_p::T, K::Integer) where T <: Real
    _logaddexp(a, b) = a == -Inf ? b : b == -Inf ? a : max(a, b) + log1p(exp(-abs(a - b)))
    lp  = [k < nb_r ? T(-Inf) : PhaseTypeDistributions.negbin_total_logpdf(k, nb_r, nb_p) for k in 1:K]
    lsf = similar(lp)                    # log P(W ≥ k), accumulated from the tail
    acc = T(-Inf)
    for k in K:-1:1
        acc = _logaddexp(acc, lp[k])
        lsf[k] = acc
    end
    h = [isfinite(lsf[k]) ? exp(lp[k] - lsf[k]) : zero(T) for k in 1:K]
    h[end] = one(T)
    return clamp.(h, zero(T), one(T))
end
```

# Boxcar SIR simulation

The Boxcar model represents the infectious period with explicit infection-age cohorts: newly infected individuals enter the first age class, then move through $r$ classes one step at a time, leaving each class according to the NegBin hazard. Its incidence term, $\beta(\sum I)S$, matches the GLCT forward map. So for a fixed $(\beta,\rho)$ and dwell-time distribution, the two formulations induce the same epidemic trajectory and should produce equivalent posteriors on the same data.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

function sir_boxcar_map!(du, u, p, t)
    (β, h, K, Δt) = p
    Tel = eltype(u)
    S = u[1]
    ΣI = sum(u[2:K+1])
    R = u[K+2]
    # Probability-per-step infection update (hazard -> event probability).
    p_inf = rate_to_proportion(β * ΣI, Δt)
    new_inf = p_inf * S
    du[1] = S - new_inf
    du[K+2] = R
    @inbounds begin
        du[2] = new_inf
        for k in 2:K
            du[k+1] = zero(Tel)
        end
    end
    @inbounds for k in 1:K
        current_I = u[k+1]
        leave = current_I * h[k]
        stay = current_I - leave
        if k < K
            du[k+2] += stay
        end
        du[K+2] += leave
    end
    return nothing
end

function simulate_boxcar(β, h_rec, ρ, nsteps, K_age_classes, Δt)
    Tel = promote_type(typeof(β), eltype(h_rec), typeof(ρ))
    u0 = zeros(Tel, K_age_classes + 2)
    u0[1] = one(Tel) - ρ
    u0[2] = ρ
    u0[K_age_classes+2] = zero(Tel)
    sol = zeros(Tel, K_age_classes + 2, nsteps + 1)
    sol[:, 1] = u0
    p = (β, h_rec, K_age_classes, Δt)
    for t in 2:(nsteps+1)
        u_next = zeros(Tel, length(u0))
        sir_boxcar_map!(u_next, sol[:, t-1], p, t - 1)
        # NUTS + ForwardDiff can explore extreme parameters; keep S,I,R nonnegative and
        # S on [0,1] so τ = S(0)−S(T) stays finite (avoids NaN Dual in Binomial(N,τ)).
        u_next[1] = max(zero(Tel), min(one(Tel), u_next[1]))
        u_next[K_age_classes+2] = max(zero(Tel), u_next[K_age_classes+2])
        @inbounds for i in 2:(K_age_classes+1)
            u_next[i] = max(zero(Tel), u_next[i])
        end
        sol[:, t] = u_next
    end
    τ = u0[1] - sol[1, end]
    f = zeros(Tel, nsteps)
    for tt in 1:nsteps
        f[tt] = tt == 1 ? sol[1, 1] - sol[1, 2] : sol[1, tt] - sol[1, tt+1]
    end
    if sum(f) > 0
        f = f / sum(f)
    else
        f = fill(one(Tel)/nsteps, nsteps)
    end
    return sol, τ, f
end
```

# Discrete GLCT simulation

The GLCT forward map iterates the discrete SIR system using the phase-type transition matrix for the infectious period. At each step, new infections are distributed across infection stages according to the initial probability vector $\alpha$, existing infections advance through the sub-transition matrix $T$, and absorptions accumulate in the recovered class. The incidence probability mass function is obtained from the successive decrements in $S$.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

function simulate_discrete_glct(Tm::AbstractMatrix, α::AbstractVector, β::Real, ρ::Real, nsteps::Int, Δt::Real)
    k = length(α)
    @assert size(Tm, 1) == k == size(Tm, 2) "Tm must be k×k"
    S = 1.0 - ρ
    x = α .* ρ
    R = zero(ρ)
    S_hist = Any[S]
    I_hist = Any[sum(x)]
    R_hist = Any[R]
    times = collect(0.0:Δt:(nsteps*Δt))
    for _ in 1:nsteps
        I = sum(x)
        # Probability-per-step infection update (hazard -> event probability).
        p_inf = rate_to_proportion(β * I, Δt)
        new_inf = p_inf * S
        x = Tm' * x + α .* new_inf
        absorption_probs = ones(eltype(α), k) - Tm * ones(eltype(α), k)
        recov = dot(absorption_probs, x)
        S = S - new_inf
        R = R + recov
        push!(S_hist, S)
        push!(I_hist, sum(x))
        push!(R_hist, R)
    end
    τ = S_hist[1] - S_hist[end]
    dS = diff(S_hist)
    f = max.(-dS, 0.0)
    sF = sum(f)
    f = sF > 0 ? f ./ sF : fill(one(eltype(f))/length(f), length(f))
    return (times=times, S=S_hist, I=I_hist, R=R_hist, τ=τ, f=f)
end
```

# Synthetic line list

The synthetic dataset is generated in three steps: the deterministic GLCT forward map produces the final attack rate $\tau$ and incidence PMF $f$; the observed final size $K$ is then drawn from $\text{Binomial}(N,\tau)$ and individual infection times from $\text{Multinomial}(K,f)$; and each infectious period $\delta_i$ is sampled from the Erlang-4 DPH by inverse CDF. All three scenarios condition on the same single realisation of $(K, \mathbf{th}, \boldsymbol{\delta})$.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

function generate_discrete_glct_data(β, Tm, α, ρ, N, M, n_events, Δt; rng::Union{Nothing,Random.AbstractRNG}=nothing)
    result = simulate_discrete_glct(Tm, α, β, ρ, n_events, Δt)
    τ = result.τ
    f = result.f
    K = isnothing(rng) ? rand(Binomial(N, τ)) : rand(rng, Binomial(N, τ))
    if K > 0 && length(f) > 0
        if length(f) != n_events
            f = f[1:n_events]
        end
        if sum(f) > 0
            f = f / sum(f)
        else
            f = fill(1.0/n_events, n_events)
        end
        th = isnothing(rng) ? rand(Multinomial(K, f)) : rand(rng, Multinomial(K, f))
    else
        th = zeros(Int, n_events)
    end
    delta = Int[]
    if M + K > 0
        dph = PhaseTypeDistributions.DPH(α, Tm)
        for _ in 1:(M + K)
            u = isnothing(rng) ? rand() : rand(rng)
            cum_prob = 0.0
            recovery_time = 1
            while cum_prob < u
                pmf_val = PhaseTypeDistributions.pmf(dph, recovery_time)
                cum_prob += pmf_val
                cum_prob >= u && break
                recovery_time += 1
            end
            push!(delta, recovery_time)
        end
    end
    return Dict(:K => K, :th => th, :delta => delta, :τ => τ, :f => f)
end
```

# Turing models

The following subsections define the Turing.jl probabilistic models for each scenario and infectious-period representation. All models share the same discrete epidemic forward map and differ only in which likelihood components are active and which parameters are estimated.

## Scenario A — Full data ($\ell_I + \ell_R + \ell_\text{constr}$)

Scenario A uses the complete likelihood: the incidence histogram and final size constrain the transmission parameters $(\beta, \rho)$, while the individual recovery intervals identify the infectious period shape $(r, p)$. With all three data streams present, the integer phase count $r$ is summed out of the likelihood over its prior support, and NUTS samples $(\beta, \rho, p)$.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""Full-data log-likelihood for a given phase count `nb_r` (GLCT map, NegBin DPH)."""
function dph_full_loglik(nb_r, β, ρ, nb_p, N, M, nsteps, K, th, delta, Δt)
    any(<(nb_r), delta) && return -Inf   # outside the NegBin support {r, r+1, ...}
    (0 < nb_p < 1) || return -Inf        # support of p (an extreme NUTS proposal can underflow p to 0)
    dph     = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r, nb_p)
    result  = simulate_discrete_glct(dph.S, dph.α, β, ρ, nsteps, Δt)
    τ_valid = clamp(result.τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(result.f, nsteps)
    ll = logpdf(Binomial(N, τ_valid), K)
    if K > 0
        all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01 || return -Inf
        ll += logpdf(Multinomial(K, f_safe), th)
    end
    return ll + sum(logpdf(dph, delta[i]) for i in 1:(M + K))
end

@model function dph_full(N::Int, M::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int,
                          th::Vector{Int}, delta::Vector{Int},
                          nb_r_max::Int, Δt::Float64)
    # NegBin-DPH; Binomial/Multinomial for epidemic data; delta ~ DPH.
    # nb_r ~ DiscreteUniform(1, nb_r_max) is summed out (one forward-map run per value).
    β    ~ Uniform(1e-4, β_prior_hi)
    ρ    ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    nb_p ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)
    logmarg, lps = marginal_r_loglik(1:nb_r_max) do nb_r
        dph_full_loglik(nb_r, β, ρ, nb_p, N, M, nsteps, K, th, delta, Δt)
    end
    Turing.@addlogprob! logmarg
    return lps   # per-r log-likelihoods, used to draw nb_r after sampling
end
```

## Scenario B — Infection times only, summed over $r$

Scenario B uses only the infection-time likelihood $\ell_I + \ell_\text{constr}$. The phase count $r$ is summed out over $\{1, \ldots, r_{\max}\}$. The sampled parameters are $R_0$, the mean infectious period $\mu$ and $\rho$, with $p = r/\mu$ and $\beta = R_0 p / r = R_0/\mu$ derived for each $r$. This keeps $(R_0, \mu)$ meaningful across all values of $r$; with $(R_0, p)$ sampled instead, the same $p$ implies a different mean IP for every $r$, and the summed posterior mixes poorly.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""Infection-only log-likelihood (final size + incidence) for a given phase count `nb_r`,
with p = r/μ and β = R₀/μ."""
function dph_infonly_loglik(nb_r, R₀, μ, ρ, N, nsteps, K, th, Δt)
    nb_p = nb_r / μ
    (0 < nb_p < 1) || return -Inf       # mean IP must exceed the minimum duration r
    dph     = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r, nb_p)
    result  = simulate_discrete_glct(dph.S, dph.α, R₀ / μ, ρ, nsteps, Δt)
    (isfinite(result.τ) && all(isfinite, result.f)) || return -Inf
    τ_valid = clamp(result.τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(result.f, nsteps)
    ll = binomlogpdf(N, τ_valid, K)     # AD-safe; avoids Binomial(N,p) constructor on Dual types
    if K > 0
        all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01 || return -Inf
        ll += logpdf(Multinomial(K, f_safe), th)
    end
    return ll
end

@model function dph_infonly(N::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int, th::Vector{Int},
                             nb_r_max::Int, Δt::Float64)
    R₀      ~ Uniform(0.5, 5.0)
    mean_ip ~ Uniform(1.0, 30.0)        # mean infectious period (days)
    ρ       ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    # nb_r ~ DiscreteUniform(1, nb_r_max) is summed out
    logmarg, lps = marginal_r_loglik(1:nb_r_max) do nb_r
        dph_infonly_loglik(nb_r, R₀, mean_ip, ρ, N, nsteps, K, th, Δt)
    end
    Turing.@addlogprob! logmarg
    return lps
end
```

## Scenario C — Recovery times only ($\ell_R$)

Without infection time data, the transmission rate $\beta$ and initial fraction $\rho$ are not identified. We estimate only the infectious period distribution parameters $(r, p)$ directly from recovery intervals.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

@model function dph_reconly(delta::Vector{Int}, nb_r_max::Int)
    # nb_r ~ DiscreteUniform(1, nb_r_max) is summed out
    nb_p    ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)
    logmarg, lps = marginal_r_loglik(1:nb_r_max) do nb_r
        any(<(nb_r), delta) && return -Inf
        (0 < nb_p < 1) || return -Inf    # support of p
        dph = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r, nb_p)
        sum(logpdf(dph, d) for d in delta)
    end
    Turing.@addlogprob! logmarg
    return lps
end
```

## Scenario C — Recovery times only (Geometric baseline)

The Geometric model for recovery-only inference estimates $p$ from $\delta_i$ directly. Since Geometric $\equiv$ NegBin$(r=1)$ has a single parameter, this is a NUTS-only run with no Metropolis-Hastings step required.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

@model function geo_reconly(delta::Vector{Int})
    nb_p ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)
    dph_geo = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_geometric(nb_p)
    for i in 1:length(delta)
        delta[i] ~ dph_geo
    end
    return (nb_p=nb_p,)
end
```

## Geometric baseline — Scenario A ($\ell_I + \ell_R + \ell_\text{constr}$)

The geometric model is the memoryless special case of the NegBin DPH, equivalent to a single exponential infectious stage ($r=1$). Fitting it alongside the DPH model under the full likelihood quantifies the cost of assuming exponential dwell times when the true infectious period has lower coefficient of variation.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

@model function geo_full(N::Int, M::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int,
                          th::Vector{Int}, delta::Vector{Int},
                          Δt::Float64)
    β    ~ Uniform(1e-4, β_prior_hi)
    ρ    ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    nb_p ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)

    if !(0 < nb_p < 1)                   # support of p (an extreme NUTS proposal can underflow p to 0)
        Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf
        return (β=β, nb_p=nb_p, ρ=ρ, τ=0.0)
    end
    dph_geo = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_geometric(nb_p)
    result  = simulate_discrete_glct(dph_geo.S, dph_geo.α, β, ρ, nsteps, Δt)
    τ_valid = clamp(result.τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(result.f, nsteps)

    K ~ Binomial(N, τ_valid)
    if K > 0
        if all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01
            th ~ Multinomial(K, f_safe)
        else
            Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf
        end
    end
    for i in 1:(M + K)
        delta[i] ~ dph_geo
    end

    return (β=β, nb_p=nb_p, ρ=ρ, τ=τ_valid)
end
```

## Geometric baseline — Scenario B ($\ell_I + \ell_\text{constr}$)

Under Scenario B, the geometric model requires no shape selection step since $r \equiv 1$ is fixed by definition. This provides a clean infection-only baseline against which the GLCT and Boxcar results can be compared.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

@model function geo_infonly(N::Int, M::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int,
                             th::Vector{Int}, Δt::Float64)
    β    ~ Uniform(1e-4, β_prior_hi)
    ρ    ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    nb_p ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)

    if !(0 < nb_p < 1)                   # support of p (an extreme NUTS proposal can underflow p to 0)
        Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf
        return (β=β, nb_p=nb_p, ρ=ρ, τ=0.0)
    end
    dph_geo = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_geometric(nb_p)
    result  = simulate_discrete_glct(dph_geo.S, dph_geo.α, β, ρ, nsteps, Δt)
    τ_valid = clamp(result.τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(result.f, nsteps)

    K ~ Binomial(N, τ_valid)
    if K > 0
        if all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01
            th ~ Multinomial(K, f_safe)
        else
            Turing.@addlogprob! -Inf
        end
    end
    # NO recovery likelihood

    return (β=β, nb_p=nb_p, ρ=ρ, τ=τ_valid)
end
```

## Boxcar — Scenario A ($\ell_I + \ell_R + \ell_\text{constr}$)

The Boxcar model is the infection-age representation of the same NegBin DPH likelihood. Its state space has dimension $K_\text{age}+2$ (vs $r+2$ for DPH), but it is mathematically equivalent. Both correctly-specified models should produce identical posteriors on the same data.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""Full-data log-likelihood for a given phase count `nb_r` (Boxcar map, same NegBin DPH)."""
function boxcar_full_loglik(nb_r, β, ρ, nb_p, N, M, nsteps, K, th, delta, K_age_classes, Δt)
    any(<(nb_r), delta) && return -Inf
    (0 < nb_p < 1) || return -Inf        # support of p
    dph_bc  = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r, nb_p)
    h_rec   = hazard_vector_negbin(nb_r, nb_p, K_age_classes)
    _, τ, f = simulate_boxcar(β, h_rec, ρ, nsteps, K_age_classes, Δt)
    (isfinite(τ) && all(isfinite, f)) || return -Inf
    τ_valid = clamp(τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(f, nsteps)
    ll = binomlogpdf(N, τ_valid, K)  # AD-safe Binomial
    if K > 0
        all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01 || return -Inf
        ll += logpdf(Multinomial(K, f_safe), th)
    end
    return ll + sum(logpdf(dph_bc, delta[i]) for i in 1:(M + K))
end

@model function boxcar_full(N::Int, M::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int,
                             th::Vector{Int}, delta::Vector{Int},
                             K_age_classes::Int, nb_r_max::Int, Δt::Float64)
    β    ~ Uniform(1e-4, β_prior_hi)
    ρ    ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    nb_p ~ Beta(1.0, 1.0)
    # nb_r ~ DiscreteUniform(1, nb_r_max) is summed out, as in dph_full
    logmarg, lps = marginal_r_loglik(1:nb_r_max) do nb_r
        boxcar_full_loglik(nb_r, β, ρ, nb_p, N, M, nsteps, K, th, delta, K_age_classes, Δt)
    end
    Turing.@addlogprob! logmarg
    return lps
end
```

## Boxcar model for Scenario B ($\ell_I + \ell_\text{constr}$, summed over $r$)

The infection-only Boxcar model mirrors the DPH Scenario B specification, with the GLCT transition matrix replaced by infection-age cohort dynamics. This cross-checks that the two representations remain consistent when recovery data are absent.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

"""Infection-only Boxcar log-likelihood for a given phase count `nb_r` (p = r/μ, β = R₀/μ)."""
function boxcar_infonly_loglik(nb_r, R₀, μ, ρ, N, nsteps, K, th, K_age_classes, Δt)
    nb_p = nb_r / μ
    (0 < nb_p < 1) || return -Inf
    h_rec   = hazard_vector_negbin(nb_r, nb_p, K_age_classes)
    _, τ, f = simulate_boxcar(R₀ / μ, h_rec, ρ, nsteps, K_age_classes, Δt)
    (isfinite(τ) && all(isfinite, f)) || return -Inf
    τ_valid = clamp(τ, 0.001, 0.999)
    f_safe  = safe_normalise(f, nsteps)
    ll = binomlogpdf(N, τ_valid, K)
    if K > 0
        all(x -> isfinite(x) && !isnan(x), f_safe) && abs(sum(f_safe) - 1) < 0.01 || return -Inf
        ll += logpdf(Multinomial(K, f_safe), th)
    end
    return ll
end

@model function boxcar_infonly(N::Int, nsteps::Int, K::Int, th::Vector{Int},
                                K_age_classes::Int, nb_r_max::Int, Δt::Float64)
    R₀      ~ Uniform(0.5, 5.0)
    mean_ip ~ Uniform(1.0, 30.0)
    ρ       ~ Beta(1.0, N - 1)
    logmarg, lps = marginal_r_loglik(1:nb_r_max) do nb_r
        boxcar_infonly_loglik(nb_r, R₀, mean_ip, ρ, N, nsteps, K, th, K_age_classes, Δt)
    end
    Turing.@addlogprob! logmarg
    return lps
end
```

# Data generation

The synthetic dataset is generated from the nominal parameters defined above. The printed output reports the observed final size $K$, the empirical mean and coefficient of variation of the recovery intervals, and the Boxcar truncation length required to cover the worst-case prior tail under Scenario B.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

# N = susceptibles followed, M = pre-study infected
N_sim  = 99
M_sim  = 1
ρ_sim  = ρ_true

data_fwd = generate_discrete_glct_data(β_true, dph_nom.S, dph_nom.α, ρ_sim,
                                        N_sim, M_sim, nsteps, Δt_nom)
K_obs      = data_fwd[:K]
th_obs     = data_fwd[:th]
delta_obs  = data_fwd[:delta]
τ_true_det = data_fwd[:τ]
f_true_det = data_fwd[:f]

nb_r_max_data = minimum(delta_obs)

# K_age_B: Boxcar state-space length for Scenario B; worst-case prior is Geometric(1/30)
# (r=1, mean=30 d), whose 99.9th percentile sets the required truncation.
dph_worst_B = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(1, 1.0/30.0)
K_age_B     = findfirst(k -> PhaseTypeDistributions.cdf(dph_worst_B, k) >= 0.999, 1:500)

println("Simulator: β_true=$β_true per Δt, k=$nb_r, μ_ip=$μ_ip d (CT mean input), E[W]=$(round(nb_mean,digits=3)) d, R₀_imp=$(round(R0_imp, digits=3)), τ_det=$(round(τ_true_det, digits=3))")
println("Observed: K=$K_obs / N=$N_sim  (attack rate $(round(K_obs/N_sim, digits=3)))")
println("Recovery: mean=$(round(mean(delta_obs), digits=2)) d, " *
        "min=$(minimum(delta_obs)), max=$(maximum(delta_obs)), " *
        "CV=$(round(std(delta_obs)/mean(delta_obs), digits=3))")
println("nb_r_max_data = $nb_r_max_data,  K_age = $K_age  (Scenario A),  K_age_B = $K_age_B  (Scenario B Boxcar)")
```

# MCMC inference

All NegBin DPH and Boxcar models (Scenarios A, B and C) sum the integer phase count $r$ out of the likelihood and are sampled with NUTS alone: four chains, each started from jittered data-based values (see the code below), with 1,000 warm-up and 2,000 posterior draws per chain (4,000 for Scenario B, whose wide and correlated posterior over $R_0$ and the mean infectious period needs more draws to reach $\hat{R} < 1.01$). After sampling, each draw is paired with one draw of $r$ from its exact conditional posterior, which is added to the chain as `:nb_r`.

The geometric fits (Scenarios A, B and C, $r \equiv 1$) have no integer parameters and use the same sampler settings: four chains from jittered data-based values, 1,000 warm-up and 2,000 draws per chain.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

nb_r_max   = 10        # upper bound for DiscreteUniform prior on nb_r (Scenarios A, Boxcar A)
Δt_val     = Δt_nom  # must match simulator time step (here: 1 day per step)

# Scenarios A, C and Boxcar A: nb_r summed out; NUTS with 4 chains from data-based starts
n_samples_int  = 2000
n_samples_B    = 4000   # Scenario B: wide, correlated (R₀, μ) posterior needs more draws for R̂ < 1.01
nuts_adapt_int = 1000
n_chains       = 4
nuts_int       = NUTS(nuts_adapt_int, 0.8; max_depth=12, Δ_max=1000.0)
# Chains start from jittered data-based values (Methods): R0 from the final-size relation R0 = −log(1 − K/N)/(K/N),
# the per-stage probability p from the recovery intervals as p = min δ / mean δ (the largest admissible phase count
# over the mean interval; 1/mean δ for the geometric model), ρ at its prior median, and the mean IP at its prior
# median where no recovery intervals are used (Scenario B). Each value is multiplied by exp(0.1 z), z ~ N(0, 1), per chain.
init_rng = Xoshiro(20261006)
function data_inits(model, n)
    z = K_obs / N_sim; R0h = clamp(-log(1 - z) / z, 0.6, 4.9); ip = mean(delta_obs); ρh = median(Beta(1.0, N_sim - 1))
    p_nb = clamp(minimum(delta_obs) / ip, 1e-3, 0.99)
    j() = exp(0.1 * randn(init_rng))
    f = model.f
    map(1:n) do _
        if f === dph_full || f === boxcar_full
            InitFromParams((β = j() * R0h / ip, ρ = j() * ρh, nb_p = clamp(j() * p_nb, 1e-3, 0.99)))
        elseif f === dph_infonly || f === boxcar_infonly
            InitFromParams((R₀ = clamp(j() * R0h, 0.55, 4.95), mean_ip = j() * 15.5, ρ = j() * ρh))
        elseif f === dph_reconly
            InitFromParams((nb_p = clamp(j() * p_nb, 1e-3, 0.99),))
        elseif f === geo_full
            InitFromParams((β = j() * R0h / ip, ρ = j() * ρh, nb_p = clamp(j() / ip, 1e-3, 0.99)))
        elseif f === geo_infonly
            InitFromParams((β = j() * R0h * 0.5, ρ = j() * ρh, nb_p = clamp(j() * 0.5, 1e-3, 0.99)))
        elseif f === geo_reconly
            InitFromParams((nb_p = clamp(j() / ip, 1e-3, 0.99),))
        else
            error("no data-based initial values defined for $(f)")
        end
    end
end

"""Standard sampler: NUTS, `n_chains` chains from jittered data-based starts, MCMCChains output."""
sample_std(model; n_draws = n_samples_int) =
    sample(model, nuts_int, MCMCThreads(), n_draws, n_chains;
           progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains, initial_params=data_inits(model, n_chains))

"""Sample `model` (which returns per-r log-likelihoods) and add posterior draws of nb_r
(support 1:r_max) to the chain."""
function sample_summing_r(model; n_draws = n_samples_int)
    ch = sample_std(model; n_draws = n_draws)
    r_draws = [sample_index(lps) for lps in returned(model, ch)]
    return add_draws(ch, :nb_r, r_draws)
end

"""Add a matrix of derived draws (iterations × chains) to a chain under `name`."""
add_draws(ch, name, draws) =
    hcat(ch, setrange(Chains(reshape(draws, size(draws, 1), 1, :), [name]), range(ch)))


```

## Scenario A — Full DDSA (DPH)

Scenario A uses all three data streams: $\ell_I + \ell_R + \ell_\text{constr}$. With full data, the phase count $r$ is identifiable from recovery intervals: the NegBin recovery likelihood discriminates sharply between different $r$ values, so its posterior (recovered after sampling) concentrates on one value.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

model_A = dph_full(N_sim, M_sim, nsteps, K_obs, th_obs, delta_obs, nb_r_max, Δt_val)
_ = sample(model_A, nuts_int, 1; progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains)
t_A = @elapsed chain_A = sample_summing_r(model_A)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

println("Scenario A (Full DPH): $(round(t_A, digits=1)) s")
```

## Scenario B — Infection-only DDSA (DPH)

With recovery intervals absent, the posterior of $r$ is expected to be spread over several values. Summing over $r$ carries that uncertainty into the posteriors of $R_0$ and the mean infectious period, instead of conditioning on one selected value.

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

model_B = dph_infonly(N_sim, nsteps, K_obs, th_obs, nb_r_max, Δt_val)
_ = sample(model_B, nuts_int, 1; progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains)
t_B = @elapsed chain_B = sample_summing_r(model_B; n_draws = n_samples_B)
# Derived p = r/μ for each draw (used by the summaries and posterior predictive checks)
chain_B = add_draws(chain_B, :nb_p, Array(chain_B[:nb_r]) ./ Array(chain_B[:mean_ip]))
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

println("Scenario B (DPH, infection-only, summed over r): $(round(t_B, digits=1)) s")
println("Scenario B posterior P(r): ",
        round.([mean(vec(chain_B[:nb_r]) .== r) for r in 1:nb_r_max], digits=3))
```

## Scenario C — Recovery-only DDSA (DPH)

Scenario C uses only the recovery likelihood $\ell_R$. With recovery data alone, $r$ is identifiable: the likelihood is summed over $r \in \{1, \ldots, r_\text{max\_data}\}$ where $r_\text{max\_data} = \min(\delta_i)$ (the data-derived upper bound; NegBin total-trials support is $\{r, r+1, \ldots\}$).

```{julia}
#| echo: true
#| output: false

model_C = dph_reconly(delta_obs, nb_r_max_data)
_ = sample(model_C, nuts_int, 1; progress=false, chain_type=MCMCChains.Chains)
t_C = @elapsed chain_C = sample_summing_r(model_C)
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

r_selected_C = round(Int, median(vec(chain_C[:nb_r])))
println("Scenario C: inferred nb_r = $r_selected_C  (Erlang k = $nb_r)")
```

# Results

## Posterior summaries

The table below reports posterior medians and 95% credible intervals for the transmission coefficient $\beta$, mean infectious period $r/p$, phase count $r$, and $R_0 = \beta \cdot r/p$ under all scenarios and infectious-period models. $R_0$ is computed draw by draw and then summarised; in Scenario B the NegBin DPH and Boxcar models sample it directly. Medians are used rather than means because the mean infectious period can have a long right tail: under infection-only data the geometric model's $1/p$ has rare draws of hundreds of days, which make posterior means, and products of means, vary from run to run even when the chains have converged. All estimates are compared to the simulator's discrete-time targets: $\beta_\text{true} = 0.5$ per step, $E[W] \approx 6.33$ d, and $R_0^\text{imp} = 3.164$.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

mean_ip_nb(chain) = vec(chain[:nb_r]) ./ vec(chain[:nb_p])
"""Posterior median and 95% credible interval of a vector of draws."""
summ(v; digits = 3) = "$(round(median(v), digits=digits)) [$(round(quantile(v, 0.025), digits=digits)), $(round(quantile(v, 0.975), digits=digits))]"
rmode(chain) = round(Int, median(vec(chain[:nb_r])))

# Per-draw quantities for every model
β_A_draws    = vec(chain_A[:β]);      ip_A_draws   = mean_ip_nb(chain_A);   R0_A_draws   = β_A_draws .* ip_A_draws
β_Abc_draws  = vec(chain_Abc[:β]);    ip_Abc_draws = mean_ip_nb(chain_Abc); R0_Abc_draws = β_Abc_draws .* ip_Abc_draws
β_Ag_draws   = vec(chain_Ageo[:β]);   ip_Ag_draws  = 1 ./ vec(chain_Ageo[:nb_p]); R0_Ag_draws = β_Ag_draws .* ip_Ag_draws
β_Bg_draws   = vec(chain_Bgeo[:β]);   ip_Bg_draws  = 1 ./ vec(chain_Bgeo[:nb_p]); R0_Bg_draws = β_Bg_draws .* ip_Bg_draws
ip_C_draws   = mean_ip_nb(chain_C)
# Scenario B (NegBin DPH, Boxcar): R₀ and μ are sampled, β = R₀/μ; r is summed out
R0_B_draws        = vec(chain_B[:R₀]);     mean_ip_B_draws   = vec(chain_B[:mean_ip]);   β_B_draws   = R0_B_draws ./ mean_ip_B_draws
R0_Bbc_draws      = vec(chain_Bbc[:R₀]);   mean_ip_Bbc_draws = vec(chain_Bbc[:mean_ip]); β_Bbc_draws = R0_Bbc_draws ./ mean_ip_Bbc_draws
Pr(chain) = round.([mean(vec(chain[:nb_r]) .== r) for r in 1:nb_r_max], digits=2)

println("Truth: β = $β_true per step, E[W] = $(round(nb_mean, digits=2)) d, R₀_imp = $(round(R0_imp, digits=3))")
println("Posterior median [95% CrI]")
for (label, β, ip, R0, r) in (
        ("A  NegBin DPH          ", β_A_draws,   ip_A_draws,        R0_A_draws,   "r = $(rmode(chain_A))"),
        ("A  Geometric (misspec.)", β_Ag_draws,  ip_Ag_draws,       R0_Ag_draws,  "r ≡ 1"),
        ("A  Boxcar              ", β_Abc_draws, ip_Abc_draws,      R0_Abc_draws, "r = $(rmode(chain_Abc))"),
        ("B  NegBin DPH          ", β_B_draws,   mean_ip_B_draws,   R0_B_draws,   "r median $(rmode(chain_B)); P(r) = $(Pr(chain_B))"),
        ("B  Geometric (misspec.)", β_Bg_draws,  ip_Bg_draws,       R0_Bg_draws,  "r ≡ 1"),
        ("B  Boxcar              ", β_Bbc_draws, mean_ip_Bbc_draws, R0_Bbc_draws, "r median $(rmode(chain_Bbc)); P(r) = $(Pr(chain_Bbc))"))
    println("  $label  β = $(summ(β))   mean IP = $(summ(ip; digits=2)) d   R₀ = $(summ(R0; digits=2))   $r")
end
println("  C  NegBin DPH            β not identified   mean IP = $(summ(ip_C_draws; digits=2)) d   R₀ not identified   r = $(rmode(chain_C))")
println("  C  Geometric             mean IP = $(summ(1 ./ vec(chain_Cgeo[:nb_p]); digits=2)) d")
println()
println("Geometric mean-IP tails (why medians are reported): max 1/p = $(round(maximum(ip_Ag_draws), digits=1)) d (A), $(round(maximum(ip_Bg_draws), digits=1)) d (B); ",
        "mean vs median of 1/p in B: $(round(mean(ip_Bg_draws), digits=2)) vs $(round(median(ip_Bg_draws), digits=2)) d")
```

## Posterior density comparison: transmission rate β

Figure 1 compares the marginal posterior for $\beta$ across scenarios that include epidemic dynamics (Scenario C does not identify $\beta$). Under the full likelihood, all three infectious-period models concentrate near the true value. Under Geometric misspecification, the posterior shifts toward larger $\beta$ in both Scenarios A and B, because the model compensates for the wrong period shape by inflating the transmission coefficient. With recovery intervals (Scenario A) the mean infectious period stays near its true value, so $R_0$ is inflated as well. With infection times only (Scenario B) the model also shortens the mean infectious period, and $R_0$ stays close to the value implied by the observed final size.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#| label: fig-beta-scenarios

p_beta = density(vec(chain_A[:β]), label="A: Full (DPH)",
                  color=:royalblue, linewidth=2.5,
                  xlabel="β (per Δt)", ylabel="Posterior density",
                  title="Transmission coefficient β (one day per Δt)")
density!(p_beta, β_B_draws, label="B: Infection-only (DPH)",
          color=:royalblue, linewidth=2.5, linestyle=:dash)
density!(p_beta, vec(chain_Ageo[:β]), label="A: Full (Geometric)",
          color=:red3, linewidth=2.5, alpha=0.75)
density!(p_beta, vec(chain_Bgeo[:β]), label="B: Geometric (r≡1)",
          color=:red3, linewidth=2.5, linestyle=:dash, alpha=0.75)
density!(p_beta, vec(chain_Abc[:β]), label="A: Full (Boxcar)",
          color=:green4, linewidth=2.5, alpha=0.75)
density!(p_beta, β_Bbc_draws, label="B: Infection-only (Boxcar)",
          color=:green4, linewidth=2.5, linestyle=:dash, alpha=0.75)
vline!(p_beta, [β_true], color=:black, linestyle=:dot, linewidth=2.5,
        label="Simulator β (per Δt)")
plot(p_beta, size=(800, 420), left_margin=4Plots.mm, bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)
```

## Posterior density comparison: mean infectious period

Figure 2 compares the marginal posterior for mean infectious period across scenarios and infectious-period models. In Scenario A (full data), all three models concentrate near the simulator’s discrete mean, $E[W]\approx 6.33$ d, showing that the mean is well identified when recovery intervals are observed. Scenario B posteriors are wider, reflecting the lower information content of incidence data alone and the uncertainty in $r$, which is carried into the DPH and Boxcar fits by summing over it; the Geometric model adjusts through its single parameter $1/p$. Scenario C (recovery only) gives the sharpest posterior for the mean because it uses individual recovery durations directly, without epidemic-dynamics terms. When recovery intervals are observed (Scenarios A and C), the geometric model recovers the correct mean despite misspecifying the distributional shape, because the mean recovery duration identifies it. With infection times only (Scenario B) it does not: its mean infectious period is roughly half the true value, offset by a larger $\beta$. The distributional shape is identified only by the full spread of individual recovery intervals.

## Posterior for nb_r (phase count): identifiability across scenarios

Figure 3 shows the marginal posterior of the phase count $r$ in each scenario, recovered after sampling from its exact conditional distribution. In Scenario A (full data), the posterior concentrates near the simulator’s Erlang stage count $k=4$, indicating that recovery intervals provide enough information to identify shape. Scenario C (recovery only) gives a similar posterior on $r$, summed over the admissible integers $r \le \min_i \delta_i$. In Scenario B, the posterior of $r$ is spread over several values, since infection-only likelihood terms cannot sharply distinguish shapes independently of the other epidemic parameters. The vertical dotted line marks the simulator value $k=4$ in each panel.

## Posterior predictive checks

Figure 5 shows posterior predictive checks: incidence curves for Scenarios A and B, and recovery-interval histograms for Scenario C. For each posterior draw, we run the discrete epidemic forward map to obtain a predicted infection-time distribution, simulate new case counts, and overlay the posterior mean and 95% predictive interval on the observed histogram. For Scenario C, we evaluate the predicted recovery-interval distribution under inferred phase-type parameters and compare it directly with observed individual durations. Boxcar posterior predictives use the same infection-age state dimension as the corresponding fitted model to keep inference and prediction aligned.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true
#| label: fig-ppc-scenarios

function posterior_predictive_check(chain, N, nsteps; n_post=400, nb_r_default::Int=1)
    n_chain = size(chain, 1)
    idx     = round.(Int, range(1, n_chain, length=min(n_post, n_chain)))
    means   = zeros(length(idx), nsteps)
    draws   = zeros(length(idx), nsteps)
    for (i, s) in enumerate(idx)
        ρ_s    = chain[:ρ][s]
        nb_r_s = :nb_r in names(chain) ? Int(chain[:nb_r][s]) : nb_r_default
        nb_p_s = chain[:nb_p][s]
        if :R₀ in names(chain)
            R₀_s = chain[:R₀][s]
            β_s  = R₀_s * nb_p_s / nb_r_s
        else
            β_s = chain[:β][s]
        end
        dph_s  = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r_s, nb_p_s)
        r      = simulate_discrete_glct(dph_s.S, dph_s.α, β_s, ρ_s, nsteps, Δt_val)
        f_s    = (r.f); τ_s = clamp(r.τ, 0.001, 0.999)
        means[i, :] .= N .* τ_s .* max.(f_s, 0.0)
        K_new = rand(Binomial(N, τ_s))
        if K_new > 0 && all(isfinite, f_s)
            f_safe = max.(f_s, 0.0); sf = sum(f_safe)
            sf > 1e-10 && (f_safe ./= sf)
            draws[i, :] .= rand(Multinomial(K_new, f_safe))
        end
    end
    return means, draws
end

"""Incidence PPC using the Boxcar forward map (state dimension must match the inference model)."""
function posterior_predictive_check_boxcar(chain, N, nsteps, K_age_classes; n_post=400, nb_r_default::Int=1)
    n_chain = size(chain, 1)
    idx     = round.(Int, range(1, n_chain, length=min(n_post, n_chain)))
    means   = zeros(length(idx), nsteps)
    draws   = zeros(length(idx), nsteps)
    for (i, s) in enumerate(idx)
        ρ_s    = chain[:ρ][s]
        nb_r_s = :nb_r in names(chain) ? Int(chain[:nb_r][s]) : nb_r_default
        nb_p_s = chain[:nb_p][s]
        if :R₀ in names(chain)
            R₀_s = chain[:R₀][s]
            β_s  = R₀_s * nb_p_s / nb_r_s
        else
            β_s = chain[:β][s]
        end
        h_rec = hazard_vector_negbin(nb_r_s, nb_p_s, K_age_classes)
        _, τ_raw, f_raw = simulate_boxcar(β_s, h_rec, ρ_s, nsteps, K_age_classes, Δt_val)
        τ_s = clamp(τ_raw, 0.001, 0.999)
        f_s = collect(f_raw)
        (length(f_s) == nsteps && all(isfinite, f_s) && isfinite(τ_s)) || continue
        f_s = max.(f_s, 0.0)
        sf = sum(f_s)
        sf > 1e-10 && (f_s ./= sf)
        means[i, :] .= N .* τ_s .* f_s
        K_new = rand(Binomial(N, τ_s))
        if K_new > 0
            draws[i, :] .= rand(Multinomial(K_new, f_s))
        end
    end
    return means, draws
end

function fit_panel(means, draws, title_str; color=:royalblue)
    tt   = 1:nsteps
    pmd  = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.5), means, dims=1))
    plo  = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.025), draws, dims=1))
    phi  = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.975), draws, dims=1))
    p = bar(tt, th_obs;
            label     = "Observed",
            color     = :lightgray,
            linecolor = :gray,
            linewidth = 0.3,
            bar_width = 1.0,
            xlabel    = "Day index t (Δt = 1 day)",
            ylabel    = "New infection count",
            title     = title_str,
            legend    = :topright)
    plot!(p, collect(tt), plo; fillrange=phi, fillalpha=0.4, color=color,
          linewidth=0, label="95% CrI")
    plot!(p, collect(tt), pmd; color=color, linewidth=2.5, label="Posterior median")
    return p
end

"""
Posterior predictive check for recovery intervals (Scenario C).
For each posterior draw compute the expected count at each interval value
under the inferred NegBin(nb_r, nb_p) distribution and compare with the
observed histogram.
"""
function posterior_predictive_recovery(chain, delta_obs; n_post=400, nb_r_default::Int=1)
    n_chain  = size(chain, 1)
    idx      = round.(Int, range(1, n_chain, length=min(n_post, n_chain)))
    d_min    = minimum(delta_obs)
    d_max    = maximum(delta_obs) + 5
    bins     = d_min:d_max
    n_obs    = length(delta_obs)
    hist_obs = [sum(delta_obs .== k) for k in bins]
    preds    = zeros(length(idx), length(bins))
    for (i, s) in enumerate(idx)
        nb_r_s = :nb_r in names(chain) ? Int(chain[:nb_r][s]) : nb_r_default
        nb_p_s = chain[:nb_p][s]
        (0 < nb_p_s ≤ 1) || continue
        dph_s = PhaseTypeDistributions.dph_negative_binomial(nb_r_s, nb_p_s)
        for (j, k) in enumerate(bins)
            lp = logpdf(dph_s, k)
            preds[i, j] = isfinite(lp) ? n_obs * exp(lp) : 0.0
        end
    end
    return collect(bins), hist_obs, preds
end

function recovery_fit_panel(bins, hist_obs, preds, title_str; color=:royalblue)
    pmd = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.5), preds, dims=1))
    plo = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.025), preds, dims=1))
    phi = vec(mapslices(x -> quantile(x, 0.975), preds, dims=1))
    p = bar(bins, hist_obs;
            label     = "Observed",
            color     = :lightgray,
            linecolor = :gray,
            linewidth = 0.3,
            bar_width = 1.0,
            xlabel    = "Recovery interval δ (days)",
            ylabel    = "Individuals (count)",
            title     = title_str,
            legend    = :topright)
    plot!(p, collect(bins), plo; fillrange=phi, fillalpha=0.4, color=color,
          linewidth=0, label="95% CrI")
    plot!(p, collect(bins), pmd; color=color, linewidth=2.5, label="Posterior median")
    return p
end

# --- Incidence PPCs (scenarios A and B: epidemic dynamics present) ---
means_A,   draws_A   = posterior_predictive_check(chain_A,    N_sim, nsteps)
means_B,   draws_B   = posterior_predictive_check(chain_B,    N_sim, nsteps)
means_Ag,  draws_Ag  = posterior_predictive_check(chain_Ageo, N_sim, nsteps)
means_Bg,  draws_Bg  = posterior_predictive_check(chain_Bgeo, N_sim, nsteps)
means_Abc, draws_Abc = posterior_predictive_check_boxcar(chain_Abc, N_sim, nsteps, K_age)
means_Bbc, draws_Bbc = posterior_predictive_check_boxcar(chain_Bbc, N_sim, nsteps, K_age_B)

# --- Recovery interval PPCs (Scenario C: recovery times only) ---
# C-Boxcar ≡ C-DPH for recovery intervals (same NegBin model)
bins_C,  hist_C,  preds_C  = posterior_predictive_recovery(chain_C,    delta_obs)
bins_Cg, hist_Cg, preds_Cg = posterior_predictive_recovery(chain_Cgeo, delta_obs)

pA_ppc   = fit_panel(means_A,   draws_A,   "A: Full (DPH)";                  color=:royalblue)
pB_ppc   = fit_panel(means_B,   draws_B,   "B: Infection-only (DPH)";        color=:royalblue)
pAg_ppc  = fit_panel(means_Ag,  draws_Ag,  "A: Full (Geometric)";            color=:red3)
pBg_ppc  = fit_panel(means_Bg,  draws_Bg,  "B: Geometric (r≡1)";            color=:red3)
pAbc_ppc = fit_panel(means_Abc, draws_Abc, "A: Full (Boxcar)";               color=:green4)
pBbc_ppc = fit_panel(means_Bbc, draws_Bbc, "B: Infection-only (Boxcar)";     color=:green4)
pC_ppc   = recovery_fit_panel(bins_C,  hist_C,  preds_C,
                               "C: Recovery-only (DPH/Boxcar)";  color=:royalblue)
pCg_ppc  = recovery_fit_panel(bins_Cg, hist_Cg, preds_Cg,
                               "C: Recovery-only (Geometric)";   color=:red3)

# Layout: rows = scenario (A / B / C), columns = model (DPH / Geometric / Boxcar).
# Bottom-right slot is empty: C-Boxcar ≡ C-DPH (identical recovery model).
fig_ppc = plot(pA_ppc,   pAg_ppc,  pAbc_ppc,
     pB_ppc,   pBg_ppc,  pBbc_ppc,
     pC_ppc,   pCg_ppc;
     layout           = (3, 3),
     size             = (1200, 960),
     dpi              = 300,
     background_color = :white,
     left_margin      = 4mm,
     bottom_margin    = 4mm,
     top_margin       = 2mm)

let
    figdir = joinpath("..", "figures")   # repository-level figures/ folder (not tracked)
    mkpath(figdir)
    out = joinpath(figdir, "fig_data_avail_ppc.pdf")
    savefig(fig_ppc, out)
    println("Saved -> $out")
end
fig_ppc
```

## Convergence 

The diagnostics below are computed from four chains for every fit. The ESS reported is the bulk ESS for the parameter with the lowest ESS among non-constant parameters, which identifies the bottleneck for Monte Carlo accuracy. Tags such as `[nb_r=4 (const)]` indicate that a parameter was excluded from the ESS scan because its stored trace has numerically zero variance (for example, posterior draws of $r$ concentrating entirely on one integer). The recovery-only DPH scenario (C) often yields the lowest ESS on $p$, because $r$ is effectively fixed by the data while $p$ can be weakly identified or correlated with the discrete-$r$ prior support; the Geometric variant can appear better simply because it has one fewer discrete parameter. 

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: true

for (label, chain) in [("A-Full-DPH",      chain_A),
                        ("B-InfOnly-DPH",   chain_B),
                        ("C-RecOnly-DPH",   chain_C),
                        ("A-Full-Geo",      chain_Ageo),
                        ("B-Geo (r≡1)",     chain_Bgeo),
                        ("C-RecOnly-Geo",   chain_Cgeo),
                        ("A-Full-Boxcar",   chain_Abc),
                        ("B-InfOnly-Boxcar", chain_Bbc)]
    all_params  = names(chain, :parameters)
    # Constant chains (e.g. posterior draws of nb_r all equal to 4) can cause ESS to loop infinitely. Filter them out before summarystats.
    non_const   = filter(p -> std(vec(Array(chain[p]))) > 1e-10, all_params)
    const_parms = setdiff(all_params, non_const)

    const_note = ""
    if !isempty(const_parms)
        parts = map(const_parms) do p
            mode_val = round(Int, median(vec(Array(chain[p]))))
            "$p=$mode_val (const)"
        end
        const_note = " [" * join(parts, ", ") * "]"
    end

    if isempty(non_const)
        println("$label: all parameters constant$const_note")
        continue
    end

    sub_chain   = chain[:, non_const, :]
    s           = DataFrame(summarystats(sub_chain))
    pnames      = s.parameters
    rhat_finite = filter(isfinite, collect(skipmissing(s.rhat)))
    rhat_max    = isempty(rhat_finite) ? NaN : maximum(rhat_finite)
    ess_col     = s.ess_bulk
    valid       = findall(x -> !ismissing(x) && !isnan(x), ess_col)
    if isempty(valid)
        println("$label: max R̂ = $(round(rhat_max, digits=4)), ESS = N/A$const_note")
        continue
    end
    ess_min, i = findmin(collect(skipmissing(ess_col[valid])))
    worst_par  = pnames[valid[i]]
    println("$label: max R̂ = $(round(rhat_max, digits=4)), " *
            "ESS = $(round(Int, ess_min)) ($worst_par)$const_note")
end
```

# Discussion

The analysis of these scenarios demonstrates how different data types influence each model's ability to estimate epidemic parameters.

- _Scenario A (Full Data)_: When both epidemic timing and individual recovery times are known, all parameters are clearly identified. The timing of cases defines the transmission rate $\beta$, while the variation in recovery times defines the duration and shape of the infectious period.
- _Scenario B (Incidence Only):_ This scenario relies on the total number of cases and the daily incidence histogram. Without recovery data, the shape of the infectious period is poorly identified: several different shapes produce similar-looking daily case counts, so the posterior of $r$ is spread over several values, and summing over it widens the posteriors for $R_0$ and the mean infectious period. A simpler Geometric model is also tested here, which assumes a constant probability of recovery each day.
- _Scenario C (Recovery Only):_ This focuses on how long individuals stay sick, using records like hospital stays. While this data identifies the infectious period, it tells us nothing about how fast the disease spreads.

We compared two mathematical methods for tracking infections: the DPH method and the Boxcar method. Both are mathematically equivalent and produce the same results. The DPH method is more computationally efficient (using fewer states), while the Boxcar method is more intuitive but requires more processing power and longer warmup periods during estimation to reach accurate results.

Using the wrong model for the infectious period (e.g., a Geometric model) often goes unnoticed if we only look at daily case counts. At the aggregate level, the epidemic curve is driven by the product $R_0 \approx \beta r/p$. Thus, a misspecified model compensates by adjusting $\beta$ and $p$ to maintain the same $R_0$, generating a misleadingly good fit to case counts. However, the mismatch becomes apparent when examining individual recovery times. A Geometric model assumes most people recover very quickly, whereas the simulated data show a humped distribution in which most people recover after a few days.
